github.abstract: Modern Web Guidance (Source) This repo is the source repository for GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance and includes the code and documentation for authoring, calibrating, and evaluating its contents. Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. See CONTRIBUTING.md and GOVERNANCE.md for how we work on the project and orientation of the codebase. Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community. Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue Quickstart npx modern-web-guidance@latest install This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below. Try it out (without installing) # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search " animate a dialog modal backdrop " # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve " animate-to-from-top-layer " # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap. Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: Modern Browser APIs : Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. Performance & Accessibility : Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. Responsible Fallbacks : Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are designed to be token-efficient ; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. Core Disciplines 🎨 User Experience Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color ). 📐 CSS Layout Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid , modern color spaces like oklch , text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming). ⚡ Performance Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield ). 📝 Forms & UI Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields). ♿ Accessibility Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability). 🤖 Built-in AI Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs). View an example: the navigation-drawer guide . github.title: NVIDIA/SkillSpector
github.abstract:
SkillSpector Security scanner for AI agent skills. Detect vulnerabilities, malicious patterns, and security risks before installing agent skills. Overview AI agent skills (used by Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, etc.) execute with implicit trust and minimal vetting. In the 31,132-skill analyzed subset of the research dataset, 26.1% of skills contain vulnerabilities and 5.2% show likely malicious intent . SkillSpector helps you answer: "Is this skill safe to install?" SkillSpector is part of the NVIDIA Verified Skills pipeline , which scans, evaluates, and signs agent skills before publication. Skills that pass are published to the NVIDIA skills catalog . Documentation Scan agent skills before installation — Hosted guide: when to scan, how to read a report, and how to gate installs. Development guide — Architecture, package layout, and how to extend the analyzer pipeline. Security policy — Report suspected vulnerabilities privately to NVIDIA PSIRT. Analysis resource bounds — Fail-closed bundle, parser, nested-artifact, ledger, and finding ceilings. Pi extension — Install SkillSpector as a Pi tool for scanning skills from inside agent sessions. OpenCode extension — Install SkillSpector as an OpenCode tool and /skillspector command for scanning skills from inside agent sessions. Features Multi-format input : Scan Git repos, URLs, zip files, directories, or single files 71 vulnerability patterns across 17 categories: prompt injection, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, supply chain, excessive agency, output handling, system prompt leakage, memory poisoning, tool misuse, rogue agent, anti-refusal, trigger abuse, dangerous code (AST), taint tracking, YARA signatures, MCP least privilege, and MCP tool poisoning Two-stage analysis : Fast static analysis + optional LLM semantic evaluation Live vulnerability lookups : SC4 queries OSV.dev for real-time CVE data with automatic offline fallback Multiple output formats : Terminal, JSON, Markdown, and SARIF reports Risk scoring : 0-100 score with severity labels and clear recommendations Baseline / false-positive suppression : Accept known findings via a glob-rule or fingerprint baseline so re-scans surface only new issues ( docs ) Quick Start Installation Open-source software notice: This project will download and install additional third-party open source software projects. Review the license terms of these open source projects before use. Create and activate a virtual environment first (all make targets assume the venv is active). Use uv or pip ; the Makefile uses uv if available, otherwise pip . Quick install with uv (CLI-only): uv tool install git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git # Update later: uv tool update skillspector If you plan to run skillspector mcp , install the MCP extra at install time: uv tool install ' skillspector[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git ' From source: # Clone the repository git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git cd skillspector # Create and activate virtual environment uv venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # or: python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # Install for production use make install To contribute, follow the Development setup for a supported Python
interpreter and development dependencies. Docker (no Python required) Run SkillSpector without installing Python by building it locally from the included Dockerfile . The image is based on the Docker Official Python 3.12-slim-bookworm image. Build the image: make docker-build # or: docker build -t skillspector . Scan a local directory by mounting your current directory into /scan , the container's working directory: docker run --rm -v " $PWD :/scan " skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm Scan with LLM analysis by passing credentials with a local .env file: cat > .env << ' EOF ' SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER=anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... EOF docker run --rm \
  -v " $PWD :/scan " \
  --env-file .env \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/ Or pass credentials directly from your shell environment: docker run --rm \
  -v " $PWD :/scan " \
  -e SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER=anthropic \
  -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY= " $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY " \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/ Write a report to the host filesystem by writing to the mounted directory: docker run --rm --user " $( id -u ) : $( id -g ) " \
  -v " $PWD :/scan " \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm --format json --output report.json Optional alias for repeated static scans: alias skillspector-docker= ' docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/scan" skillspector ' skillspector-docker scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm Basic Usage # Scan a local skill directory skillspector scan ./my-skill/ # Scan a single SKILL.md file skillspector scan ./SKILL.md # Scan a Git repository skillspector scan https://github.com/user/my-skill # Scan a zip file skillspector scan ./my-skill.zip Size limits SkillSpector enforces two independent caps on remote and archive inputs to bound the impact of oversized downloads and zip bombs: Per-ingest cap : INGEST_MAX_BYTES (100 MiB) — applied to streamed URL downloads, total uncompressed size of zip archives, and post-clone disk usage of Git repos. Zip member cap : INGEST_MAX_ZIP_MEMBERS (10,000) — caps the number of entries in a single zip. Note that the per-file 1 MB analysis cap ( MAX_FILE_BYTES ) is a separate, downstream limit: it bounds what individual analyzers will read out of an already-ingested directory. The ingest caps above bound how much content can land on disk in the first place. A breach of either ingest cap fails closed with an IngestLimitExceededError . Output Formats # Terminal output (default) - pretty formatted skillspector scan ./my-skill/ # JSON output - machine readable skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format json --output report.json # Markdown output - for documentation skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format markdown --output report.md # SARIF output - for CI/CD integration and IDE tooling skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format sarif --output report.sarif Recursive Collection Scanning --recursive scans immediate subdirectories containing SKILL.md as independent
skills, with a default aggregate limit of 32 skills . To raise or lower it: skillspector scan ./my-skills/ --recursive --max-skills 100 --no-llm --format json --max-skills requires a local recursive collection and a positive integer; 0 does not mean unlimited. Discovery, byte, finding-record, time and report-size
budgets still apply, so increasing the count does not guarantee complete coverage.
When the count limit is reached, the CLI names the limit and suggests adjusting it
or scanning sub-skills separately. Omitted skills remain visible in the aggregate
report and coverage stays incomplete. Use --fail-on-incomplete in CI to fail on
incomplete coverage; the default exit policy is unchanged. Batch Scanning Scan entire directories of skills in parallel from contrib/batch_scan/ : python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./my-skills/ --no-llm
python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./my-skills/ --workers 20 -f json -o report.json
python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./tests/fixtures/ -f terminal --workers 20 Supports multilingual detection (zh/ja/ko) and terminal/JSON/Markdown output. For LLM scans with higher concurrency, configure multiple API keys following .env.example — the pool improves throughput
and resilience, provided the keys don't share an account-level rate limit. See the contrib guide for details. Note on LLM support: The default configuration targets DeepSeek as the
cheapest public option. DeepSeek-Chat is expected to sunset , and the contributor
does not have hardware to test against local models. The batch scanner was
originally tested with OpenAI-compatible endpoints — DeepSeek's lack of
structured-output support required manual JSON-parsing patches. If you can
contribute a more universal backend (Ollama, vLLM, or a different provider),
PRs are very welcome.

github.abstract:
OpenBot AI coworkers. Ready for the enterprise. A modular, self-hostable workspace for AI coworkers. Choose your models. Bring your agents. Own your infrastructure. open.bot · Docs · Deploy on Kubernetes · Run from source Notarized .dmg for Apple silicon and Intel Macs · signed installer for Windows x64 · no terminal or developer tools needed · Release notes From CopilotKit , creators of AG-UI . openbot-readme-demo-v2.mp4 Watch a Bot use its browser and tools, answer with interactive results, and wait for your approval before it sends. Take over when it needs you, and connect the agents you already run. Getting started On your laptop The easiest way to get started is with the fully self-contained app that runs on your laptop, combining the OpenBot frontend and Docker-based backend in one application. Mac / Apple silicon · Mac / Intel · Windows Run from source For your team OpenBot for Business brings your agents into one workspace with company sign-in, tool permissions, approvals, and audit. Deploy on your infrastructure or work with our engineers on hosting and customization. Get early access to OpenBot for Business → · Talk to an engineer · Kubernetes setup Web, mobile, and chat Web · iOS · Android · Slack · Teams Your workspace. Your stack. Choose your models. Use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, or open models through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, hosted by a provider or on your own infrastructure. Keep your provider relationships and change models as your needs change. Bring your agents. Run built-in Bots in the OpenBot server, or connect your existing agents through AG-UI from any agent execution platform. Agents built with different stacks can work in the same workspace. Make it yours. Use the MIT-licensed template as-is, white-label it, or customize it deeply. AG-UI connects agents, MCP connects tools, and the frontends and backend can evolve independently. Govern work across your team. Company sign-in, roles, tool permissions, approvals, and audit apply across the workspace. Your agents use OpenBot's tools and computers under the same policies. Get help deploying it. CopilotKit's engineers can work with your team to deploy OpenBot, connect your systems, and automate parts of specific jobs. Connect your agent · Configure models and tools · Explore OpenBot for Business Built on CopilotKit and AG-UI OpenBot is built on CopilotKit , which is used in production by a majority of Fortune 500 companies . Your agent stack. AG-UI has first-class integrations across the major agent frameworks and harnesses, including Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework and Agent Harness, Google ADK, AWS Strands, Oracle Agent Spec, LangChain, Mastra, Pydantic AI, Agno, and CrewAI. Many ship first-party support; Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supports AG-UI directly . Your execution platform. Keep your agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Managed Agents, Google's Agent Platform , LangChain's Managed Deep Agents, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service , or your own infrastructure. Connect them to OpenBot through an AG-UI endpoint, using an adapter where needed. Your choice of agent platform stays independent of your workspace. Architecture OpenBot has three parts. On your laptop, setup runs the backend and Intelligence for you. For a team, the Helm chart deploys both on Kubernetes in your own infrastructure. Part What it does OpenBot frontends Mac, Windows, web, iOS, Android, Slack, and Teams connect people to the same workspace. Conversations, interactive results, computer view, and approvals adapt to each surface. Choose a frontend . OpenBot backend Runs the workspace API and built-in Bots, connects external agents and tools, manages Bot computers, and enforces identity, permissions, action policies, and audit. Deploys on Kubernetes with PostgreSQL and persistent storage. CopilotKit Intelligence Durable conversations, memory, Automatic Learning, and enterprise governance services. Separately licensed; runs on Kubernetes alongside OpenBot. OpenBot enforces sign-in, tool permissions, action policies, and audit at its API, alongside Intelligence's platform services. Built-in Bots run in the OpenBot server; your own agents can run alongside OpenBot or on any agent execution platform. Both use AG-UI and can share the same workspace. Computer execution is pluggable: use the default Kubernetes setup or connect a compatible external computer provider. Architecture details · Services and ports · Kubernetes deployment Open source, local operation, and licensing The OpenBot application template is open source under the MIT license . You can fork, modify, and white-label it. It uses CopilotKit Intelligence , which is separately licensed and can run entirely on your own machine or infrastructure. Where you run it CopilotKit Intelligence license Your laptop, for personal use and experimentation Requires a free local Intelligence license. Desktop setup handles this for you. Kubernetes evaluation Requires a free Intelligence trial license. Request a trial . Kubernetes / production Requires a production Intelligence license beyond evaluation. OpenBot for Business includes Intelligence for use with OpenBot. Plans and pricing . Fully local is an option. Run OpenBot, Intelligence, and a compatible model locally. A cloud model or connected online app still sends requests to that service. Initial downloads, account sign-in, and local license renewal need internet access. Deploy on Kubernetes Deploy OpenBot and CopilotKit Intelligence together on AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE, or your own Kubernetes cluster . The chart installs Intelligence by default; no separate hosted project is required. For a first evaluation, you need a cluster with amd64 nodes , a default StorageClass , kubectl , Helm, a trial or production license , and a model key. The commands below use an OpenAI key. For Anthropic, a model router, cluster sizing, or an existing Intelligence deployment, use the full Helm guide . Setting up with an AI assistant? Give it this README and the Helm guide . The guide covers cloud-specific values, storage, secrets, sign-in, networking, upgrades, and troubleshooting. Use the evaluation below only through a local port-forward; configure sign-in and TLS before sharing a deployment. Get the source. Skip this if you already have a checkout. git clone https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot.git cd OpenBot Create openbot-secrets.yaml locally. Replace the placeholders with your license and model key. Keep this file out of source control. secrets : licenseToken : " <your CopilotKit trial or production license> " modelApiKey : " <your OpenAI API key> " Install. helm dependency build charts/openbot
helm install openbot charts/openbot \
  --namespace openbot --create-namespace \
  --values charts/openbot/ci/vanilla-values.yaml \
  --values openbot-secrets.yaml \
  --timeout 15m Open your evaluation. kubectl -n openbot get pods,jobs
kubectl -n openbot port-forward svc/openbot-server 3001:3001 Open http://127.0.0.1:3001 . This configuration is single-user: anyone who can reach it is an administrator. Keep the port-forward local. The chart creates the runtime credentials, installs the databases, bootstraps Intelligence, and sets up the Learning container and scheduled jobs. Automatic Learning uses your model key too. For a team deployment, follow the Helm guide to configure authentication, TLS, your database, secrets, persistent storage, and network policies. For a single-container alternative, see Deploy it . Run from source Use the template to customize the workspace, branding, Bots, and skills. The source setup below uses managed Intelligence by default; local Intelligence is also available. git clone https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot.git cd OpenBot Requirements To run the open-source template locally, you’ll need the following. Docker, for PostgreSQL and the shipped Bots. Bun 1.4+, for the app, the API server and the tests (some tests fail on 1.3).

Key Capabilities AI-Native Automation Platform : Build and operationalize AI workflows and multi-step agents using your own data, models, and tools Model Flexibility, No Lock-In : Connect to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or open-source models and switch providers without changing your architecture From Prototype to Production : Design multi-step AI workflows with logic, tool use, human approvals, and full observability Code When You Need It : Combine visual building with JavaScript, Python, and npm packages for advanced AI workflows Enterprise-Ready AI : Self-host or deploy securely with role-based access, audit trails, and support for sensitive data Leverage What Already Exists : 1500+ integrations and 9,000+ workflow templates to connect AI with your existing systems Quick Start Try n8n instantly with our install script (requires Docker ): curl -fsSL https://get.n8n.io | sh Or deploy manually with Docker : docker volume create n8n_data
docker run -it --rm --name n8n -p 5678:5678 -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n Access the editor at http://localhost:5678 Resources 📚 Documentation 🔧 1500+ Integrations 💡 Example Workflows 🤖 AI & LangChain Guide 👥 Community Forum 📖 Community Tutorials Support Need help? Our community forum is the place to get support and connect with other users: community.n8n.io License n8n is fair-code distributed under the Sustainable Use License and n8n Enterprise License . Source Available : Always visible source code Self-Hostable : Deploy anywhere Extensible : Add your own nodes and functionality Enterprise Licenses available for additional features and support. Additional information about the license model can be found in the docs . Contributing Found a bug 🐛 or have a feature idea ✨? Check our Contributing Guide for a setup guide & best practices. Join the Team Want to shape the future of automation? Check out our job posts and join our team! What does n8n mean? Short answer: It means "nodemation" and is pronounced as n-eight-n. Long answer: "I get that question quite often (more often than I expected) so I decided it is probably best to answer it here. While looking for a good name for the project with a free domain I realized very quickly that all the good ones I could think of were already taken. So, in the end, I chose nodemation. 'node-' in the sense that it uses a Node-View and that it uses Node.js and '-mation' for 'automation' which is what the project is supposed to help with. However, I did not like how long the name was and I could not imagine writing something that long every time in the CLI. That is when I then ended up on 'n8n'." - Jan Oberhauser, Founder and CEO, n8n.io

github.abstract: Locally Uncensored The all-in-one local AI studio for your desktop. Chat, images, video and a coding agent in one app. Install it, pick a model, go. Free and open source. In local mode everything runs on your own machine. No Docker, no terminal, no config files. The platforms are listed under Download . Download · Three steps · What is in the box · How it compares · Models · FAQ Chat that draws your images Images and video in the same window The coding agent shows the diff first Agent mode does the legwork Download Take the latest build from Releases . Platform File Status Windows 10 and 11 Locally.Uncensored_3.0.10_x64-setup.exe (NSIS, recommended) or Locally.Uncensored_3.0.10_x64_en-US.msi Tested every release, signed auto update channel Linux Locally.Uncensored_3.0.10_amd64.AppImage , Locally.Uncensored_3.0.10_amd64.deb or Locally.Uncensored-3.0.10-1.x86_64.rpm Built on every release macOS 14 or newer, Apple Silicon (Beta) LU_3.0.10_aarch64.dmg Signed with an Apple Developer ID and notarized by Apple. Intel Macs are not supported. The app has run on one Mac so far. Voice has been tried by hand in the app on a Mac and works. Computer control is in the Mac app but not fully tested yet on macOS. Remote Access and the automatic update are not confirmed on macOS Android 7.0 or newer (arm64) LU-3.0.10-Android.apk The phone app. Not in the Play Store yet: install the file from this page. SHA-256 dbd515d81bbc8ab70f21b850424f9f8b57ae88ae24962225beefc4116d139d2f Some antivirus engines flag unsigned NSIS installers that download other binaries, which is a false positive. The installer is built by GitHub Actions from the public source on master , and the update channel is signed against a public minisign key, so you can verify both: see SECURITY.md . Code signing for the Windows installers: free code signing provided by SignPath.io , certificate by SignPath Foundation . SignPath Foundation has accepted the project. The production certificate is not in place yet, and until it is the installers ship unsigned. Current release: v3.0.10 (November 2026). Every change since 1.0.0 is in CHANGELOG.md . 3.0.10 fixes lost chats from 3.0.8 and 3.0.9. A backup no longer replaces the only complete copy of your chats, a note at launch says when the backup holds chats that are missing from your list, and Settings, Chat Backup has Restore chats from backup. The Android app is back as an APK, with the keyboard staying open in the Create prompt. 3.0.9 brings Liquid's LFM3 models for small machines: 1.7B and 2B, about 1 to 1.7 GB each, for text, pictures and speech, on the LU Engine, on Ollama or as MLX builds on a Mac; the LU Engine moves to llama.cpp b11960 for them. A group chat now sends every speaker the context you picked, can redo one speaker and lets you set who speaks when. A compaction is one quiet line in the chat, and the conversation before it stays one click away. Animate takes an end image and, with MiniMax H3, up to nine reference pictures, and Krea 2, Qwen-Image 2.1 and FLUX.2 take reference pictures for a style, a person or a pose. Local videos run up to 15 seconds without drifting in colour, and a video shows a rough preview while it renders. The trainer learns a style, a concept or a pose next to a character (Beta). "Use this model" on Hugging Face opens the download in LU, and a model from the search comes in a quant that fits your graphics card. A status menu sits in the Mac menu bar and the Windows and Linux tray, and the Linux AppImage starts again on systems without the tray library. What has only run in automated tests is listed under Known limits in the release notes . 3.0.8 makes web search in the chat work again: LU asks five search services in turn and needs no key for any of them. A video made in the chat plays in the chat, and a long one renders in the background while you write on. A picture attached in the chat reaches the image tool, and with two graphics cards chat and ComfyUI can each get their own. The LU Engine plans a model's memory from the file itself and offers a shorter context with one click. AMD cards on Windows get AMD's current ROCm build. New: the chat can read and change LU's settings with a confirmation card, the Model Manager can make a copy of a local model that refuses less, and Settings, Storage puts models, gallery and runtime in one folder of your choice. What has only run in automated tests is listed under Known limits in the CHANGELOG . 3.0.5 was about Create: LTX 2.5, FastH3 and YuE2 run on your own machine, Qwen-Image 2.1 gets a transparent background and its prompt enhancer, Edit, Remove Background and Enhance Image take up to 50 images in one go, and LU Cloud adds Qwen Image 2.1, LTX 2.5, MiniMax H3 and Wan 3.0 Reference. Chat takes any file, each model in a group chat can have its own persona, dropdowns stay inside the window (issue 149), and the speech install works again on Ubuntu 24.04. 3.0.4 fixed the Code agent and the agent in chat on LU Cloud: writing a long file no longer ends the run, "continue" picks up where a run stopped instead of starting over, the agent keeps a plan only when you ask for one, and cloud context is 32K by default and can be set per model. It also fixed the bugs reported on GitHub and Discord since 3.0.3 (issues 144 to 147): MiniMax H3 runs as a video model with sound, Edit takes up to three extra images with Qwen-Image 2.1, a missing encoder or VAE is named and offered as a download instead of ending in "Value not in list", the LoRA stack follows the loras folder, and group chat works with every LU Engine model. 3.0.3 was a hotfix: chats with many images no longer run the app out of memory, Create reads a model's family from the file instead of its name, and the five bugs reported on GitHub since 3.0.2 are fixed (issues 139 to 143). 3.0.2 was a hotfix: the Code tab lost its scrollbar and its input box once a conversation grew taller than the window (issue 138, a regression in 3.0.1) and is held to the window height again, and the count of open cloud models now takes the Create Studio endpoints in, which makes it fourteen video models and seven image models. What is new in 3.0.1 Qwen-Image 2.1 runs locally on Windows and Linux. One model generates a picture from a prompt and edits one from a reference image, with no mask to paint. About 16 GB of files, ComfyUI 0.37.0 or newer, and a research license that does not allow commercial use. Models has a LoRAs tab of its own. Search CivitAI, download into ComfyUI's models/loras folder, see what is installed with its size and trigger word, and delete what you no longer want. Whisper [Blog] [Paper] [Model card] [Colab example] Whisper is a general-purpose speech recognition model. It is trained on a large dataset of diverse audio and is also a multitasking model that can perform multilingual speech recognition, speech translation, and language identification. Approach A Transformer sequence-to-sequence model is trained on various speech processing tasks, including multilingual speech recognition, speech translation, spoken language identification, and voice activity detection. These tasks are jointly represented as a sequence of tokens to be predicted by the decoder, allowing a single model to replace many stages of a traditional speech-processing pipeline. The multitask training format uses a set of special tokens that serve as task specifiers or classification targets. Setup We used Python 3.9.9 and PyTorch 1.10.1 to train and test our models, but the codebase is expected to be compatible with Python 3.8-3.11 and recent PyTorch versions. The codebase also depends on a few Python packages, most notably OpenAI's tiktoken for their fast tokenizer implementation. You can download and install (or update to) the latest release of Whisper with the following command: pip install -U openai-whisper Alternatively, the following command will pull and install the latest commit from this repository, along with its Python dependencies: pip install git+https://github.com/openai/whisper.git To update the package to the latest version of this repository, please run: pip install --upgrade --no-deps --force-reinstall git+https://github.com/openai/whisper.git It also requires the command-line tool ffmpeg to be installed on your system, which is available from most package managers: # on Ubuntu or Debian sudo apt update && sudo apt install ffmpeg # on Arch Linux sudo pacman -S ffmpeg # on MacOS using Homebrew (https://brew.sh/) brew install ffmpeg # on Windows using Chocolatey (https://chocolatey.org/) choco install ffmpeg # on Windows using Scoop (https://scoop.sh/) scoop install ffmpeg You may need rust installed as well, in case tiktoken does not provide a pre-built wheel for your platform. If you see installation errors during the pip install command above, please follow the Getting started page to install Rust development environment. Additionally, you may need to configure the PATH environment variable, e.g. export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" . If the installation fails with No module named 'setuptools_rust' , you need to install setuptools_rust , e.g. by running: pip install setuptools-rust Available models and languages There are six model sizes, four with English-only versions, offering speed and accuracy tradeoffs.
Below are the names of the available models and their approximate memory requirements and inference speed relative to the large model.
The relative speeds below are measured by transcribing English speech on a A100, and the real-world speed may vary significantly depending on many factors including the language, the speaking speed, and the available hardware. Size Parameters English-only model Multilingual model Required VRAM Relative speed tiny 39 M tiny.en tiny ~1 GB ~10x base 74 M base.en base ~1 GB ~7x small 244 M small.en small ~2 GB ~4x medium 769 M medium.en medium ~5 GB ~2x large 1550 M N/A large ~10 GB 1x turbo 809 M N/A turbo ~6 GB ~8x The .en models for English-only applications tend to perform better, especially for the tiny.en and base.en models. We observed that the difference becomes less significant for the small.en and medium.en models.
Additionally, the turbo model is an optimized version of large-v3 that offers faster transcription speed with a minimal degradation in accuracy. Whisper's performance varies widely depending on the language. The figure below shows a performance breakdown of large-v3 and large-v2 models by language, using WERs (word error rates) or CER (character error rates, shown in Italic ) evaluated on the Common Voice 15 and Fleurs datasets. Additional WER/CER metrics corresponding to the other models and datasets can be found in Appendix D.1, D.2, and D.4 of the paper , as well as the BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) scores for translation in Appendix D.3. Command-line usage The following command will transcribe speech in audio files, using the turbo model: whisper audio.flac audio.mp3 audio.wav --model turbo The default setting (which selects the turbo model) works well for transcribing English. However, the turbo model is not trained for translation tasks . If you need to translate non-English speech into English , use one of the multilingual models ( tiny , base , small , medium , large ) instead of turbo . For example, to transcribe an audio file containing non-English speech, you can specify the language: whisper japanese.wav --language Japanese To translate speech into English, use: whisper japanese.wav --model medium --language Japanese --task translate Note: The turbo model will return the original language even if --task translate is specified. Use medium or large for the best translation results. Run the following to view all available options: whisper --help See tokenizer.py for the list of all available languages. Python usage Transcription can also be performed within Python: import whisper model = whisper . load_model ( "turbo" ) result = model . transcribe ( "audio.mp3" ) print ( result [ "text" ]) Internally, the transcribe() method reads the entire file and processes the audio with a sliding 30-second window, performing autoregressive sequence-to-sequence predictions on each window. Below is an example usage of whisper.detect_language() and whisper.decode() which provide lower-level access to the model. import whisper model = whisper . load_model ( "turbo" ) # load audio and pad/trim it to fit 30 seconds audio = whisper . load_audio ( "audio.mp3" ) audio = whisper . pad_or_trim ( audio ) # make log-Mel spectrogram and move to the same device as the model mel = whisper . log_mel_spectrogram ( audio , n_mels = model . dims . n_mels ). to ( model . device ) # detect the spoken language _ , probs = model . detect_language ( mel ) print ( f"Detected language: { max ( probs , key = probs . get ) } " ) # decode the audio options = whisper . DecodingOptions () result = whisper . decode ( model , mel , options ) # print the recognized text print ( result . text ) More examples Please use the 🙌 Show and tell category in Discussions for sharing more example usages of Whisper and third-party extensions such as web demos, integrations with other tools, ports for different platforms, etc. License Whisper's code and model weights are released under the MIT License. hf.title: Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks
hf.abstract: A large-scale corpus of structured proof-supervision records derived from university mathematics textbooks improves language model mathematical reasoning by 16.7 percentage points over a base model when used for fine-tuning.

hf.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
hf.abstract: Low-bit quantized LLM agents can recover much of their task success through closed-loop guidance from a full-precision teacher, followed by unassisted student training on corrected and reference turns.

hf.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
hf.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

hf.title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents
hf.abstract: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback. A unified Reader interface supports interchangeable evidence acquisition across heterogeneous resources. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings. On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%. Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.

hf.title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference
hf.abstract: PISA and PISA-E use prompt-adaptive capability estimation to route prompts or select cost-aware ensembles, improving cost-performance trade-offs across LLM routing benchmarks.

hf.title: GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning
hf.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.

hf.title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
hf.abstract: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework.

hf.title: Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis
hf.abstract: Cross-modal representational alignment between unimodal language and vision models increases with model capability when captions are clean and informative, but remains below same-modality alignment and can exceed explicitly aligned vision-language models.

hf.title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
hf.abstract: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

hf.title: Mixed Signals: Weight-Space Programming for EEG and ECG
hf.abstract: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using 6times fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.
